notes:
Task and constraints: Generate every well-formed combination of n pairs of parentheses, 1 <= n <= 8.
Idea: Build the string with recursion over (open, close, partial). Add a ")" when close < open, and add a "(" when open < n. When both counts reach n, join the partial list and record it.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking with two counters prunes invalid prefixes at once, so only well-formed strings are ever completed.
Invariant: In every partial string the number of closing brackets never exceeds the number of opening brackets, and openings never exceed n.
Edge cases: n = 1 gives "()"; the branch order only affects output order; each call builds a new list partialRes + [...], so branches never share state.
Complexity: The number of results is the Catalan number C_n, about 4^n / n^1.5. Time is roughly O(n * C_n) for the joins, plus an extra O(n) list copy per recursive call. Space is O(n^2) for the recursion stack of lists of length up to 2n, not counting the output.

Task and constraints: All valid parenthesis strings for n pairs, n at most 8.
Idea: Backtracking with counters of remaining left and right brackets and one shared list curr. Append "(" if any left remain, append ")" if more rights remain than lefts, recurse, and pop afterwards. When both reach zero, record the joined string.
Technique and why it applies: Depth-first search with a shared path and undo (append / pop) avoids copying at every call.
Invariant: right >= left holds at every call, which guarantees a prefix can still be completed into a valid string.
Edge cases: n = 1; the base case does not return, but both further branches are false at that point so nothing breaks; the order of results is lexicographic with "(" first.
Complexity: Time is O(n * C_n) where C_n is the Catalan number, because each result costs O(n) to join. Space is O(n) for the path and recursion depth, which matches the labelled O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Same task, n at most 8.
Idea: Simulate the recursion with an explicit stack of tasks. Step 1 expands a state (left, right): it records a result when both are zero and schedules the child branches. Step 2 appends a character to curr, step 3 pops it after the branch has finished.
Technique and why it applies: Converting DFS to an iterative form with push and undo markers removes recursion depth concerns while visiting states in the same order.
Invariant: curr always equals the path of the state currently being expanded, because each append (step 2) is paired with a later pop (step 3).
Edge cases: Tasks are pushed in reverse order so the "(" branch runs first; for left < right the ")" branch is added; a state with left == 0 and right == 0 has no children.
Complexity: Time is O(n * C_n) for Catalan C_n results, each joined in O(n). Space is O(n), the maximum size of the task stack plus the path.

Task and constraints: Return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack or -1; both lengths are 1 to 10^4, lowercase letters.
Idea: For each start index i, slice haystack[i : i + len(needle)] and compare it with needle; return the first match. An empty needle returns 0 first.
Technique and why it applies: Naive substring search, simple and fast enough for lengths of 10^4.
Invariant: No start index before i produced a match.
Edge cases: Near the end the slice is shorter than the needle and simply never equals it; an empty needle returns 0 per the clarification; needle longer than haystack falls through to -1.
Complexity: Time is O(n * k) for haystack length n and needle length k, since each of n starts compares up to k characters. Space is O(k) for each temporary slice.

Task and constraints: First occurrence of needle in haystack, lengths 1 to 10^4.
Idea: Try only the start positions where the needle fits, from 0 to len(haystack) - len(needle), compare the slice with the needle and return the first match.
Technique and why it applies: Brute-force window comparison; limiting the range avoids useless slices at the tail.
Invariant: All starting positions before i were checked and failed.
Edge cases: If the needle is longer than the haystack, range() is empty and the answer is -1; this version has no empty-needle check because the constraints give length at least 1.
Complexity: Time is O(n * k) in the worst case, as the author labels it. Space is O(k) for the slice being compared.

Task and constraints: Substring search with lengths up to 10^4, lowercase letters.
Idea: Knuth-Morris-Pratt. First compute a prefix table for the pattern that gives, for each position, the longest proper border. Then scan the text, and on a mismatch fall back through the table instead of restarting.
Technique and why it applies: KMP never moves the text pointer backwards, so each text character is processed a bounded number of times.
Invariant: After handling text[i], j + 1 is the length of the longest prefix of the pattern that is a suffix of text[:i + 1].
Edge cases: An empty needle returns 0; j = -1 means no partial match; a full match when j == len(pattern) - 1 returns i - j.
Complexity: Time is O(n + k) because the fallback loop is amortized across the scan and across the table construction. Space is O(k) for the prefix table.

Task and constraints: Divide two 32-bit integers without multiplication, division or mod, truncating toward zero; result clamped to the 32-bit range.
Idea: Work with absolute values. Repeatedly double the divisor (_sum += _sum) while it still fits into the dividend, subtract the largest such multiple and add the matching power of two to the quotient. Apply the sign and clamp.
Technique and why it applies: Doubling is repeated shifting, a binary long division that needs logarithmically many subtractions.
Invariant: quotient plus dividend // divisor of the remaining dividend always equals the original quotient.
Edge cases: A divisor of 1 is handled directly; -2^31 / -1 would be 2^31, so the final min(quotient, 2147483647) clamps it; the large triple-quoted block at the top is a dead string, not code.
Complexity: Time is O(log^2 dividend), which is a constant (at most about 31 * 31 steps) for 32-bit input. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Integer division without * / % for 32-bit inputs, truncated toward zero.
Idea: Take absolute values. While the dividend still holds the divisor, subtract shifted copies of the divisor (inc doubles each time) and add the matching power of two to the result. Negate when the signs differ.
Technique and why it applies: Bit-shift subtraction is binary long division, which needs only logarithmic steps.
Invariant: result * |divisor| plus the remaining dvd equals |dividend| at every step.
Edge cases: This version has no clamp, so -2^31 divided by -1 returns 2^31, which the current statement says should be 2^31 - 1; a dividend smaller than the divisor returns 0; zero dividend returns 0.
Complexity: Time is O(log n), which is O(1) for fixed-width integers, as the author labels it. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Find all start indices in s where the concatenation of all words (any order, equal lengths) appears. s up to 10^4, up to 5000 words, each up to 30 letters.
Idea: Count the required words in a dictionary. For each start l, cut the next len(words) chunks of the word length, count the ones that are required words in curr, and compare curr with the required counts. Record l when equal.
Technique and why it applies: A brute-force window check using frequency maps; chunks that are not words are simply not counted, so the equality then fails.
Invariant: At each start, curr counts only the chunks of the current window that belong to the word set.
Edge cases: The window length must fit inside s (the while condition r < len(s) + 1); duplicate words are handled by counts; the dictionary comparison is exact.
Complexity: Time is O(m * n * k) for m start positions, n words and word length k, because every window slices n chunks of k characters and compares maps. Space is O(n * k) for the maps.

Task and constraints: Same search; at most 5000 words of length up to 30, s up to 10^4.
Idea: Build the required counts, then test every start i in range(m + 1 - k*n). Take the window chunk by chunk; stop early when a chunk is not a word or appears more often than allowed. If all n chunks pass, record i.
Technique and why it applies: Brute-force windows with an early exit, which prunes most starts quickly.
Invariant: When j == n for a start, every chunk is a required word and no word exceeded its count, so the window is an exact permutation.
Edge cases: A string shorter than n*k returns []; because the total chunks equal n and no count is exceeded, all counts must match exactly; duplicates in words are handled by counts.
Complexity: Time is O(m * n * k) in the worst case. Space is O(n * k) for the dictionaries, as the author labels it.

Task and constraints: Same problem, with s up to 10^4 and word length up to 30.
Idea: For each of the k possible offsets, slide a window over s in steps of one word. Keep counts of the words in the window; when a word is over its allowed count, move left forward one word at a time. When the count reaches n, left is a match. A non-word chunk resets the window.
Technique and why it applies: Per-offset sliding window means each word chunk enters and leaves the window once, so the work per offset is linear in m / k.
Invariant: tmp holds the counts of the chunks between left and the current chunk, and none exceeds the required count.
Edge cases: Empty words returns []; the loop stops at m - k + 1 so a chunk never runs past the end; after a non-word chunk left jumps to j + k.
Complexity: Time is O(m * k): k offsets, about m / k chunks each, and every chunk costs a k-character slice. Space is O(n * k) for the maps.

Task and constraints: Length of the longest valid parentheses substring, s up to 3 * 10^4 characters, possibly empty.
Idea: Keep a stack of indices starting with -1 as a base. Push the index of every "(". On ")" pop; if the stack becomes empty push the current index as the new base, otherwise the valid length ending here is i minus the new stack top.
Technique and why it applies: A stack of unmatched positions measures the distance back to the last unmatched index.
Invariant: The stack top is always the index just before the current valid run begins.
Edge cases: An empty string returns 0; a ")" with only the base on the stack resets the base; sequences like "(()" keep an unmatched "(" below the run.
Complexity: Time is O(n), one pass with constant stack work. Space is O(n) for the stack in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Longest valid parentheses substring, length up to 3 * 10^4.
Idea: Use a stack of indices of unmatched "(" and a variable last for the most recent unmatched ")". On ")" with an empty stack set last = i. Otherwise pop; if the stack is now empty the run length is i - last, otherwise it is i minus the new top.
Technique and why it applies: Same stack-of-positions idea with the base stored separately.
Invariant: last is the index before the current valid segment when no "(" is pending, and the stack top plays that role otherwise.
Edge cases: Empty input returns 0; a string with only closing brackets keeps updating last; leftover "(" indices stay on the stack and bound the final runs.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Space is O(n) for the stack, as the author states.

Task and constraints: Longest valid parentheses substring for a string of up to 3 * 10^4 characters.
Idea: Make two counting passes. Left to right, count depth with "(" as the opener, reset the start when depth drops below zero and record a length when depth hits zero. Then do the same right to left with ")" as the opener, and take the larger result.
Technique and why it applies: Counting scans replace the stack; the reverse pass catches runs that the forward pass misses when extra "(" remain.
Invariant: In each pass start marks the position just before the current balanced run, and depth is the excess of openers since start.
Edge cases: Empty strings return 0; a string like "(()" is solved only by the reverse pass; abs(i - start) handles both directions.
Complexity: Time is O(n), two linear passes. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Search a target in a rotated sorted array of distinct values, length up to 5000, and return its index or -1.
Idea: Binary search. At mid, check whether the left half [l, mid] is sorted. If it is, the target lies in it only if nums[l] <= target < nums[mid]; otherwise the right half is sorted and the same test is made against it. Narrow the range accordingly.
Technique and why it applies: In a rotated sorted array at least one half around mid is always sorted, which keeps the binary search valid.
Invariant: If the target exists, it lies inside [l, r].
Edge cases: A target equal to nums[mid] returns at once; the condition nums[l] <= nums[mid] covers a one-element range; an array that is not rotated works too.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) since the range halves each loop. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Find the first and last position of target in a sorted array of up to 10^5 elements in O(log n); return [-1, -1] if absent.
Idea: Use one binary search helper that returns the first index where a condition holds. The left end is the first index with nums[i] >= target. The right end is the first index with nums[i] > target, minus one.
Technique and why it applies: Two lower-bound searches on a monotone predicate give both boundaries in logarithmic time.
Invariant: In the search the answer always stays within [left, right + 1], and the predicate is false before the answer and true after.
Edge cases: An empty array returns [-1, -1] through the left == len(nums) check; a missing target is rejected by nums[left] != target; only the first helper is used, the other three are unused variants.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) for two searches. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return the index of target in a sorted array of distinct values, or the index where it would be inserted. The statement asks for O(log n).
Idea: Scan from the left and return the first index whose value is at least target; if none, return the length.
Technique and why it applies: A linear scan over a sorted array finds the lower bound, though it does not meet the logarithmic requirement of the statement.
Invariant: All values before the returned index are smaller than the target.
Edge cases: A target larger than every element returns len(nums); a target smaller than the first returns 0; an exact match returns its own index.
Complexity: Time is O(n) in the worst case, which is slower than the O(log n) the statement asks for, though n is at most 10^4. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Check that a 9 x 9 Sudoku board has no repeated digit in any row, column or 3 x 3 box; blanks are '.'.
Idea: Make three passes. Use a dictionary per row to detect repeats, then per column, then a defaultdict of lists keyed by (i // 3, j // 3) for boxes. Return False at the first repeat.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-based duplicate detection per group is the direct way to verify the three rules.
Invariant: At the time a digit is read, the set of digits already seen in its row, column or box contains only earlier cells of that group.
Edge cases: Blank cells are skipped; the code relies on defaultdict being available, which LeetCode imports for you, and it prints "TRUE1" and "TRUE2" leftovers; box membership uses a list rather than a set.
Complexity: Time is O(1) for the fixed 81 cells (O(n^2) for an n x n board). Space is O(1), bounded by 9 digits per group.

Task and constraints: Return the n-th term of the count-and-say sequence, 1 <= n <= 30.
Idea: Recursively get the previous term, then scan it, counting runs of equal digits and appending the count followed by the digit. The base case n = 1 returns "1".
Technique and why it applies: Direct simulation of the definition; each term is a run-length description of the one before.
Invariant: At the end of the scan res describes all runs processed so far, and count and cur describe the open run.
Edge cases: n = 1 returns "1"; the final run is appended after the loop; digits never exceed 3 so counts are single digits.
Complexity: Term length grows by about 30 percent per step (Conway's constant, about 1.3), so time is O(1.31^n) for the total scanning, with string concatenation assumed amortized. Space is O(1.31^n) for the strings plus O(n) recursion depth.

Task and constraints: n-th count-and-say term for n up to 30.
Idea: Start with "1" and apply getNext n - 1 times. getNext walks the string, counts the length of each run of equal digits and appends count + digit to the next sequence.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative run-length encoding of the previous term.
Invariant: After k iterations seq is the (k + 1)-th term of the sequence.
Edge cases: n = 1 returns "1" without any call; the inner while loop moves i to the last digit of each run so that the outer step advances past it.
Complexity: Time is O(n * 2^n) as the author labels it, which is a loose upper bound since each term has fewer than 2^n characters and there are n steps. Space is O(2^n) for the largest term.
